appSubtitle: Multi-Criteria Decision Analysis (MCDA) · WSM · TOPSIS · AHP · PROMETHEE II · VIKOR
taskContextDesc: Select the interchange type category to compare alternatives.
criteriaWeightsDesc: Adjust slider values. Weights are auto-normalised to sum to 1.0.
projectParamsDesc: Define site-specific constraints and traffic characteristics.
dataFooter: Data: FHWA (2023) · HCM 7th Ed. · PIARC Road Safety Manual (2022).

tapToExplore: Tap any card to explore its detailed engineering profile, metrics, and real-world map.
normDesc: Min-Max normalisation maps each raw value to [0, 1]. Minimize criteria are inverted so 1.0 denotes the best performer. Cell format: normalised x̄ᵢⱼ → weighted contribution wⱼ · x̄ᵢⱼ.
wsmDesc: The composite priority score for alternative i is computed as the weighted sum of normalised criterion values:
defSi: Composite WSM score for alternative i, Sᵢ ∈ [0, 1]
defWj: Normalised weight for criterion j, with Σwⱼ = 1
defXij: Min-max normalised value of criterion j for alternative i
minMaxDesc: Raw criterion values are mapped to the unit interval [0, 1] according to the direction of preference.
maxDir: Maximize — higher raw value is preferred (e.g. throughput, safety):
minDir: Minimize — lower raw value is preferred (e.g. cost, land area):
edgeCase: Edge case: when maxⱼ = minⱼ (all alternatives equal), the normalised score is set to 0.5.

Cloverleaf.description: Grade-separated 4-loop interchange. High capacity and free-flow operations with no traffic signals, but loop ramp geometry creates large land requirements and weaving sections between successive on/off ramps reduce safety at high volumes.
Cloverleaf.engineering_desc:
The cloverleaf interchange is a grade-separated junction where each turning movement is served by a loop ramp in one of the four quadrants. Per the **AASHTO Green Book (7th Ed.)**, loop ramp design speeds range from 25–50 km/h depending on the ramp radius.

**HCM 7th Edition (Chapter 14)** notes that weaving segments between consecutive on- and off-ramps are the primary capacity bottleneck. The effective Level of Service degrades rapidly above 3,500–4,000 veh/hr aggregate volume.

Modern practice favours *collector-distributor (C-D) roads* to mitigate weaving, effectively converting a basic cloverleaf into a *partial cloverleaf with C-D* (FHWA, 2023).
pros: Full free-flow movement — no traffic signals required
Moderate construction cost relative to directional interchanges
Well-understood design with extensive AASHTO/FHWA guidance
Simultaneous left-turn accommodation via loop ramps
cons: Large right-of-way footprint (typically 16–25 ha)
Weaving sections between successive loop ramps degrade capacity at high volumes
Low-speed loop geometry (40–55 km/h design speed) creates merge conflicts
Lower safety index due to speed differentials and weaving (PIARC, 2019)

Turbine.description: Directional interchange with semi-direct ramps arranged in a turbine pattern. Eliminates weaving conflicts, delivers superior throughput and safety, but requires significant right-of-way and construction investment.
Turbine.engineering_desc:
The turbine interchange arranges semi-direct ramps in a spiralling pattern, eliminating the weaving segments inherent in cloverleaf designs. **FHWA Interchange Justification Report Guidelines (2023)** classify turbine interchanges as a *system interchange* suitable for freeway-to-freeway junctions with projected AADT above 80,000.

Per **HCM 7th Edition**, the absence of weaving allows sustained LOS C/D operation at volumes that would push a cloverleaf into LOS E/F. The curving flyover ramps are typically designed for 60–80 km/h, significantly higher than cloverleaf loops.

Widely adopted in the Netherlands and Germany, the turbine is considered a best-practice design for high-volume, space-conscious system interchanges (PIARC Road Safety Manual, 2019).
pros: Eliminates all weaving conflicts — direct/semi-direct ramps only
High throughput capacity (5,500–7,000 veh/hr per HCM Ch. 14)
Excellent safety record — no speed-differential merge conflicts
Aesthetically efficient footprint relative to capacity delivered
cons: Significant construction cost due to multilevel flyover ramps
Larger right-of-way than stacked designs (25–30 ha typical)
Complex drainage design due to curved, elevated ramp geometry
Longer construction timeline compared to at-grade alternatives

Stack (4-Level).description: Four-level fully directional grade-separated interchange. The highest-capacity and safest system interchange type; all movements are direct with no weaving or signal delay, at the cost of maximum construction complexity.
Stack (4-Level).engineering_desc:
The four-level stack interchange provides fully directional, grade-separated connections for all turning movements using stacked flyover ramps. **FHWA (2023)** considers this the highest-capacity system interchange form, justified only when projected volumes exceed the capacity of turbine or cloverleaf alternatives.

**HCM 7th Edition (Chapter 14)** reports effective capacity of 7,000–8,500 veh/hr with sustained LOS C. The absence of weaving, loop-ramp speed differentials, and at-grade conflicts yields the highest safety index per **AASHTO Highway Safety Manual (2022)**.

The vertical stacking of four structural levels compresses the ground-level footprint to roughly 10–15 ha — considerably less than a cloverleaf serving the same volume — at the cost of significant structural engineering investment.
pros: Maximum throughput — all movements are direct with no weaving or signals
Highest safety index among system interchanges (AASHTO HSM, 2022)
Minimal land footprint for capacity delivered (10–15 ha typical)
Design speeds of 50–80 km/h on all ramps — no slow loops
cons: Highest construction cost of all interchange types (typically $60–120M+)
Maximum structural complexity — 3 or 4 bridge levels required
Visual impact and noise propagation due to elevated structures
Long construction duration (5–8 years for major urban stacks)

Diamond.description: Standard diamond interchange with four ramp terminals controlled by signals or roundabouts at the arterial crossings. Cost-effective and compact, but at-grade signal crossings introduce delay and limit peak throughput.
Diamond.engineering_desc:
The conventional diamond interchange connects a limited-access highway to an arterial via four ramp terminals — two on each side of the overpass. **AASHTO Green Book (7th Ed.)** identifies it as the default service interchange for low-to-moderate volume crossings.

Per **HCM 7th Edition (Chapter 23)**, the signalised ramp terminals are the capacity bottleneck; adaptive signal control (SCOOT/SCATS) can improve throughput by 10–15% over fixed-time plans.

**FHWA (2023)** notes that the diamond is the most cost-effective interchange where AADT is below 30,000 and left-turn volumes are moderate.
pros: Lowest construction cost of all interchange types
Minimal right-of-way requirement (3–6 ha typical)
Simple, well-understood design — rapid construction timeline
Easily retrofittable with roundabouts or adaptive signal control
cons: At-grade signal crossings limit peak throughput to ~2,500 veh/hr
Signal delay degrades LOS during peak hours (HCM Ch. 23)
Left-turn conflict points reduce safety compared to grade-separated designs
Not suitable for freeway-to-freeway (system) interchange applications

SPUI.description: Single Point Urban Interchange: all ramp movements converge at one signalised intersection. Combines near-cloverleaf throughput with a compact urban footprint, optimal for constrained corridors where land acquisition cost is critical.
SPUI.engineering_desc:
The Single Point Urban Interchange (SPUI) consolidates all ramp movements into one signalised intersection positioned directly under or over the freeway bridge. **FHWA Technical Advisory T6640.8A** recommends SPUIs where conventional diamonds exceed capacity but land constraints preclude a DDI or cloverleaf.

**HCM 7th Edition (Chapter 23)** reports that a well-designed SPUI achieves throughput of 4,000–5,000 veh/hr — nearly double a conventional diamond — through its efficient two-phase signal cycle.

The design requires a wider bridge deck (typically 40–60 m) compared to a diamond (20–30 m), increasing structural cost by 30–50% (NCHRP Report 345).
pros: Single signal phase handles all movements — high throughput for footprint
Compact urban footprint (3–5 ha typical)
Reduces conflict points vs. conventional diamond (fewer signal phases)
Strong LOS performance at moderate-to-high volumes (HCM Ch. 23)
cons: Higher construction cost than diamond due to wider bridge structure
Single-point signal failure cascades to entire interchange
Pedestrian accommodation requires careful design (FHWA Ped. Guide, 2023)
Complex signal timing — requires experienced traffic engineering

DDI.description: Diverging Diamond Interchange: traffic crosses to the opposite side of the road at two signalised crossovers, eliminating left-turn conflicts. High throughput and a strong safety record in recent North American and European deployments.
DDI.engineering_desc:
The Diverging Diamond Interchange (DDI), also known as the Double Crossover Diamond (DCD), routes traffic to the left side of the road between two signalised crossover points. This geometry eliminates all left-turn conflict points, dramatically improving safety.

**FHWA Every Day Counts (EDC-4)** promoted the DDI as a proven innovation; crash studies at early installations (e.g., I-44/Route 13, Springfield, MO) reported 40–60% reduction in total crashes.

**HCM 7th Edition** notes that the two-phase crossover signal achieves throughput comparable to a SPUI (5,000–6,000 veh/hr) at 60–70% of SPUI construction cost, making it an increasingly popular retrofit option.
pros: Eliminates left-turn conflict points — strong safety improvement (40–60% crash reduction)
High throughput with only two signal phases per crossover
Moderate construction cost — often a retrofit of existing diamond
Proven safety record: 100+ US installations since 2009 (FHWA EDC-4)
cons: Counter-intuitive driver experience at crossover points
Requires clear wayfinding signage and positive guidance markings
Slightly larger footprint than conventional diamond (5–7 ha)
Limited pedestrian/bicycle accommodation without dedicated facilities

Trumpet.description: Three-leg interchange with a loop ramp for one turning movement and direct ramps for the other two. Common for highway termini; cost-effective with a moderate footprint and good safety characteristics.
Trumpet.engineering_desc:
The trumpet interchange serves three-leg (T-junction) connections where a highway terminates or a major ramp branches. One movement uses a loop ramp while the other two use semi-direct or direct ramps.

**AASHTO Green Book (7th Ed.)** specifies trumpet interchanges for freeway termini where traffic demand on the loop movement is moderate (<1,500 veh/hr).

**HCM 7th Edition** capacity analysis shows the loop ramp governs overall interchange capacity. **PIARC (2019)** rates trumpets favourably for safety among T-junction solutions due to the limited number of conflict points.
pros: Cost-effective three-leg interchange — one loop + two direct ramps
Moderate footprint (8–12 ha typical)
Good safety for T-junction applications (AASHTO HSM, 2022)
Simple design with proven performance for highway termini
cons: One loop ramp introduces speed differential and potential weaving
Not expandable to four-leg operation without major reconstruction
Loop ramp capacity is the system bottleneck at high volumes
Limited to three-leg (T-junction) configurations only

Directional T.description: Three-leg directional interchange using semi-direct flyover ramps. Achieves maximum throughput and safety for T-junctions at the cost of higher construction expense and right-of-way requirements.
Directional T.engineering_desc:
The Directional T interchange replaces the trumpet's loop ramp with a semi-direct flyover, providing high-speed, free-flow connections for all three turning movements.

**FHWA (2023)** recommends the directional T when peak-hour turning volumes exceed the capacity of a trumpet's loop ramp (typically >2,000 veh/hr) or when the mainline design speed exceeds 100 km/h.

**HCM 7th Edition** reports that directional T interchanges sustain LOS C at volumes that would degrade a trumpet to LOS E. **AASHTO HSM (2022)** assigns the highest safety performance function (SPF) scores among T-junction designs.
pros: Maximum throughput for three-leg junctions — all movements semi-direct
Highest safety index for T-junction category (AASHTO HSM, 2022)
No loop ramp speed differentials — higher design speeds on all ramps
Scalable — can accommodate very high turning volumes (>5,000 veh/hr)
cons: High construction cost due to multilevel flyover ramps
Large right-of-way requirement (12–18 ha typical)
Complex structural engineering — multiple bridge levels
Longer construction timeline than trumpet alternatives

methodsDesc: Select the MCDA methods to run and compare.

weightingModeDesc.manual: Weights come from the sliders below.
weightingModeDesc.entropy: Criteria that vary more across the alternatives get more weight.
weightingModeDesc.critic: Weights reward contrast and penalise criteria that duplicate each other.
weightingModeDesc.ahp: Weights come from your pairwise comparisons of the criteria.

ahpHint: Above 1: the left criterion matters more (Saaty 1–9 scale).
comparisonDesc: Rank of each alternative under every selected method. Consensus is a Borda count across methods.
unanimous: All methods pick the same winner
agreementNeedsTwo: Select at least two methods to compare rankings.
methodsTheoryIntro: Every selected method ranks the same adjusted decision matrix with the same weights, so their results can be compared directly.

topsis.title: TOPSIS
topsis.desc: Columns are vector-normalised and weighted. Each alternative is scored by its relative closeness to the ideal point (best value of every criterion) and its distance from the anti-ideal point.

ahp.title: AHP — Analytic Hierarchy Process
ahp.desc: Criterion weights are the principal eigenvector of the expert pairwise comparison matrix A; judgements are accepted when the consistency ratio CR is below 0.10. Alternatives are compared by value ratios, giving local priorities p_ij that are synthesised with the weights.

promethee.title: PROMETHEE II
promethee.desc: For every pair of alternatives the difference on each criterion is turned into a preference degree P_j ∈ [0, 1] (V-shape function over the criterion's range by default). The net flow φ = leaving flow − entering flow gives a complete ranking.

vikor.title: VIKOR
vikor.desc: S measures group utility and R the worst individual regret. Q blends them with v = 0.5; lower Q is better. If the leader's advantage or stability is not acceptable, VIKOR reports a compromise set instead of a single winner.

entropy.title: Entropy weights (objective)
entropy.desc: p_ij = x_ij / Σ_i x_ij. A criterion whose values barely differ between alternatives has entropy close to 1 and receives little weight.

critic.title: CRITIC weights (objective)
critic.desc: σ_j is the standard deviation of the min-max normalised criterion and r_jk the correlation between criteria. High contrast raises a weight; strong correlation with other criteria (redundancy) lowers it.

smaa.title: SMAA-2 — stochastic acceptability
smaa.desc: Criterion values are drawn from their uncertainty ranges and weights from a distribution around the chosen weights (or uniformly). The rank acceptability b is the share of N draws in which alternative i takes rank r; central weights are the average weights that make an alternative win.

sensitivity.title: Weight sensitivity
sensitivity.desc: One weight is moved from 0 to 1 while the others keep their proportions. The stability interval is the range of that weight in which the winner does not change; its ends are the rank-reversal thresholds.

agreement.title: Rank agreement and consensus
agreement.desc: Spearman's ρ and Kendall's τ measure how similarly two methods rank the alternatives (1 = identical, −1 = reversed). The consensus ranking is a Borda count B_i over all selected methods.

robustnessDesc: Monte Carlo simulation (SMAA-2): criterion values and weights are sampled from their uncertainty ranges and every method re-ranks the alternatives on the same draws.
valueRangesDesc: How far each true value may lie below or above the expert estimate. Triangular: the estimate is most likely; uniform: every value in the range is equally likely.
weightChangeFlips: weight change that removes the lead of
noSingleFlip: No change of a single weight alters the winner.
rankAcceptabilityDesc: Share of draws in which each alternative takes each rank. Holistic acceptability weighs rank 1 fully and the last rank not at all; the confidence factor is how often the alternative wins with its own central weights.
firstByMethodTitle: Probability of ranking first, by method
firstByMethodDesc: Same draws for every method, so differences come from the method itself.
stabilityDesc: Dot: current weight. Whisker: range in which the winner stays first while the other weights keep their proportions. Labels name who takes over past each end.
sweepDesc: Score of each alternative as one weight moves from 0 to 1 (the other weights keep their proportions). Dashed: current weight; red dotted: rank-reversal thresholds.
methodLoss: VIKOR Q (lower is better, axis flipped)
siteAnalysisDesc: Click the map to pick a site. The system infers context, terrain, environmental sensitivity and free land from OpenStreetMap and elevation data, and can draw the real footprint of an interchange there.
clickToPlaceHint: Click the map to place the interchange centre.
pointAPlaced: Drag the marker to adjust the site, or click elsewhere to move it.
clickToSetDirection: Click the map to set the primary road direction…
confirmContextChange: The inferred context differs from the one currently selected. Switching will change which alternatives are being compared. Continue?
footprintSectionDesc: Draw a chosen interchange type's real footprint at this site and estimate right-of-way / demolition cost from buildings it would displace. The layout follows the primary-road direction you set (for a trumpet or directional T, the through road).

valueSourceHint.expert: Fixed expert estimates, adjusted by the site rules below.
valueSourceHint.model: Expert estimates corrected by the model trained on project documents.

modelRangesHint: Prediction-model mode: each range comes from the model’s {level}% prediction intervals and is shown read-only.
modelIntro: A grey-box Bayesian residual correction of the expert values. For every past project in the corpus it compares the documented cost, land take, capacity and safety with what the expert pipeline gives under that project’s conditions, and learns how real projects deviate by interchange type, traffic, lanes, design speed, terrain and environmental sensitivity. Predictions come with prediction intervals; with no documents the model returns the expert values unchanged. Retraining is closed-form and takes milliseconds.
modelEvaluationUses: Source of values in the evaluation
modelUseInEvaluation: Use the model in the evaluation
modelEmptyCorpus: No training records yet, so the model reproduces the expert values exactly. Upload project documents to let it learn.
modelSyntheticBadge: Synthetic records are demo data. Replace them with real project documents before relying on the predictions.
modelDocsDesc: Tables (CSV, JSON, JSONL) are read row by row; reports (TXT, MD, PDF) are parsed from “Field: value” lines. Every change retrains the model.
modelDropHint: Drop documents here or click to choose files
modelOverwriteConfirm: A document named “{name}” already exists. Replace it?
modelDeleteConfirm: Delete “{name}” and retrain the model without it?
modelEditingOffTitle: Uploading documents is turned off on this server
modelEditingOff: The corpus is read-only here: documents can’t be uploaded, deleted or retrained, but the model below and its predictions work as usual. To turn editing on, the server administrator sets an admin token (TDSS_ADMIN_TOKEN), then unlocks this panel with it.
modelUnlockHint: Uploading, deleting and retraining need the admin token set on the server. It is kept only in this browser tab, until you lock editing or close the tab.
modelLockHint: Forget the admin token in this tab
modelAccuracyDesc: Each project is predicted by a model fitted without it (leave-one-out) and compared with its documented value.
modelAccuracyNote: Error = mean absolute percentage error (lower is better); green where the model beats the expert values. Coverage = share of held-out values inside the {level}% interval, ideally close to {level}%. “—” means fewer than 3 observations. Above 200 observations, 10-fold cross-validation replaces leave-one-out.
modelChartDesc: For the selected context and project parameters: the expert value (diamond) and the model prediction (circle) with its {level}% prediction interval.
modelCoefDesc: Posterior mean and standard deviation of each correction on the log scale of documented ÷ expert value. Type rows are per-type corrections at the reference conditions (AADT 45 000, 2 lanes per direction, 100 km/h, flat terrain, low sensitivity); the other rows are slopes. Effect = e^mean − 1.
modelCoefCredible: the 90% posterior interval of the effect excludes zero (|mean| > 1.645 · SD).
scenariosDesc: Save the current inputs under a name to come back to them, compare them, or send them as a link.
scenarioCompareEmpty: Save a scenario in the Scenarios section of the inputs panel and tick it. Ticked scenarios appear here next to the current inputs.
scenarioDiffers: The input differs between the columns.
scenarioRankingDesc: Rank and WSM score in each scenario. — means the alternative is infeasible there or not part of its context.

report.title: Interchange decision report
report.noneFeasible: No alternative satisfies the budget and land limits.
report.rankingNote: Criterion values after the site adjustments. Method columns give the rank by each method; consensus is the Borda count over the methods (an alternative gets m − rank points from each).
report.agreementNote: Kendall's τ_b between the rankings: 1 = identical order, 0 = unrelated, −1 = reversed.
report.smaaIntro: {n} Monte Carlo draws of the criterion values and weights ({model}). The share of draws in which each alternative ranks first, and the probability of exceeding the budget or the land limit:

weightModels.perturbed: weights perturbed around the chosen ones

report.sensitivity: {winner} stays first unless the weight of {criterion} ({weight}) changes by more than {change}.
report.sensitivityStable: {winner} stays first for any single weight change.
report.modelEmpty: The corpus has no documents, so the model reproduces the expert values.
report.modelUsed: The values in this report come from the prediction model, trained on {n} project records. Expert value → predicted value, with the {level} % prediction interval:
report.modelReference: The values in this report are the expert constants. For reference, the prediction model trained on {n} project records gives (expert → predicted, with the {level} % prediction interval):
report.modelSynthetic: {n} of the training records are synthetic demo data.
report.footer: Generated by TDSS v5, a multi-criteria decision support system for interchange selection (WSM, TOPSIS, AHP, PROMETHEE II, VIKOR; SMAA-2 uncertainty analysis). The ranking supports, and does not replace, an engineering design review.

siteNotes.twoMinor: Two road corridors found, but neither is a motorway or trunk road. The context is a guess (the most common case); confirm it manually.
siteNotes.oneCorridor: Only one major road corridor was found near this point, and a junction needs at least two. Confirm the context manually.
siteNotes.noRoads: No major roads (tertiary or above) were found within the search radius. Confirm the context manually or widen the radius.
siteNotes.noElevationData: No usable elevation data in the search grid, so terrain defaulted to Flat. Confirm it manually.
siteNotes.elevationUnavailable: Elevation data is unavailable right now, so terrain defaulted to Flat. Confirm it manually.

study.title: Traffic and life cycle
study.desc: Design-life inputs of the traffic, safety and economic analyses. They do not change the MCDA ranking.

eng.title: Traffic and safety over the design life
eng.desc: Peak-hour traffic per interchange element (ramps, loops, weaving sections, signals) from the opening year to the design year, its volume/capacity ratio and level of service, and the expected crashes per year.
eng.site: Opening-year peak hour {v} veh/h · peak direction {q} pc/h · turning {t} pc/h · basic lane capacity {c} pc/h/ln · heavy-vehicle factor ×{hv}
eng.vcChartDesc: The interchange's most loaded element in the peak direction. Above 0.93 the element runs at LOS E; above 1.0 demand exceeds capacity and queues form.
eng.crashChart: Expected crashes over the design life
eng.crashChartDesc: Crash rate of the interchange type × entering vehicles × crash modification factors (loop ramps above 80 km/h, congestion above V/C 0.85).
eng.elementsDesc: Peak-direction volume against the capacity of each element, in the opening year and the design year. The mainline merge is the same for every alternative of this site.
eng.assumptions: Planning-level model: capacities after HCM 7 (ramp roadways, weaving, signalised terminals), BPR delay, crash rates per million entering vehicles after the HSM and FHWA studies. Constants are in app/data/engineering_defaults.py; replace them with local values on a real project.

econ.title: Life-cycle cost appraisal
econ.desc: Each alternative costed over its design life in present values: construction, maintenance and residual value for the road agency; delay and crashes for road users. Benefits are measured against the do-minimum, the feasible alternative with the lowest agency cost.
econ.basis: Discount rate {r}% · value of time ${vot}/veh·h · maintenance {m}%/yr · crash costs: fatal + injury ${fi}, property damage ${pdo} · {from}–{to}
econ.unit: All money in M USD, present values at the opening year minus one.
econ.breakdownTitle: What the life-cycle cost is made of
econ.breakdownDesc: Present values by component; the residual value at the end of the design life is credited.
econ.cumulativeDesc: Where two lines cross, the dearer alternative has paid back its extra construction cost through lower delay, crash and maintenance costs.
econ.beDesc: How good would one criterion value have to be for an alternative to rank first under the current weights? For the winner: how far could each of its values worsen before it loses first place? One value changes at a time; the others stay as they are.
econ.beHint: Not reachable means even a 20-fold change (or the end of the scale) does not change the outcome: under min–max normalisation a value beyond the best of the others gains nothing more.
econ.assumptions: Crash costs: HSM Table 4-3 comprehensive costs indexed to about 2024. Residual value: straight-line over a 50-year service life. Off-peak delay is not counted.

group.title: Group decision
group.desc: Several stakeholders each give their own criterion weights. Each one's ranking is computed with the selected methods, the weights are combined by the influence-weighted geometric mean, and agreement with the group ranking is measured with Kendall's τ.
group.name: Name
group.basisConsensus: Ranked by the Borda consensus of the selected methods.
group.kendallHint: Kendall's τ between a stakeholder's ranking and the group's: 1 the same order, 0 unrelated, −1 reversed.
group.shareDesc: Share of total influence held by the stakeholders whose first choice each alternative is.
